stops.title: Point Lines: connect and measure
stops.makes: You join A and B, compute b - a and its length, and show the distance as text while either end moves.

notes.text: The kit's `line.gd` is indented with tabs, and the code on this page uses spaces. Godot accepts either, but not both in one file. A line pasted with spaces into `line.gd` stops the whole script with `Parse Error: Used space character for indentation instead of tab as used before in the file.`, and the study runs without it: A and B sit at the middle of the floor. Indent with the Tab key instead.

Reversing the subtraction changes nothing you can see. `segment.gd` does its own subtraction from A and B, and the length is the same either way. To see the direction reverse, add `print(displacement)` on the line under `var displacement := b - a`. The Output panel fills with `(1.5, 0.0, 0.0)`, one line per frame. Change `b - a` to `a - b`, and it prints `(-1.5, 0.0, 0.0)`, while the segment and the readout stay as they were. Put back `b - a` and remove the print.

stops.title: Break it on purpose, then look it up
stops.makes: You break scripts that work, predict each error, read Godot's exact message, fix it, and look a method up in the class reference.
stops.status_note: Every message on this page comes from a Godot 4.6 run. The editor's panels are described, not watched.

verified.native: 2026-09-30 Godot 4.6, headless and with the command-line debugger (-d) driven through each stop: every case run in a fresh copy of the point-zero, point-lines or point-trace kit, every quoted message, warning, debugger stop and backtrace reproduced.

teacher.why_here: Debugging should come in through small constructions the learner already owns, not wait for an appendix. By Trace the learner has met paths, types, lists and a function that calls another, so each has a loud failure worth reading. The project's own common failures are quiet, so the loud cases come first, and the quiet ones close the workshop.
teacher.status_detail: Rewritten 2026-09-30: every case starts from a fresh kit copy; runtime cases lead with the debugger stop; the list faults moved into a point-trace copy (a wrong literal, the empty-list guard removed, pop_back for pop_front). Debugger behaviour was measured with Godot's command-line debugger, which attaches as the editor's does, by sending continue and bt through a pipe: a SCRIPT ERROR in _process stops again after each continue; one in _ready does not; ERROR lines never stop the game. Warnings (unused variable, narrowing conversion) print only with a debugger attached. The editor's Debugger panel, script editor and Search Help were not watched.
teacher.check: Each message you predicted appears, and names a line at or near the fault. Parse errors appear before the scene runs. A SCRIPT ERROR stops its function and, from the editor, pauses the game at its line; an ERROR is printed and the game goes on.
teacher.contrast: A fault with no error, such as a readout that shows the wrong number, is found by watching a value. Sometimes a warning points at it first; pop_back in the recorder leaves none.
teacher.carries: A debugging habit that starts from a prediction, the difference between an error, a warning and silence, and the class reference as the first place to look.

stops.title: Plane: when the line closes
stops.makes: You close your recorded walk into a face: a triangle fan from the list, normals, and a collider you can stand on.
stops.image_caption: The finished study, side 0 (clockwise), from above: a twelve-point walk closed into a face, lit, with its shadow on the floor; the marble waits beside it. Turned counter-clockwise the face vanishes from above and the marble still rests on it.

teacher.why_here: Operation added to the toolkit: close.
teacher.check: Axis: winding and the side the face shows - clockwise / clockwise, flipped normals / counter-clockwise / counter-clockwise, double-sided. Predict first: From above, clockwise and counter-clockwise double-sided will look most alike: both show a lit face and differ only by the shadow (measured: 0.82% of the frame). Counter-clockwise alone shows nothing from above and everything from below. Write which pair you expect before you render.
teacher.contrast: Claim: A surface has a side: what you see of a plane is a promise its winding and normals make (Godot winds front faces clockwise). Debt: Culling (Gaboury, Image Objects, 'Culling Vision'): hidden-surface algorithms decide what exists for the eye; a one-sided plane is invisible from behind while its collider still stops you. The fan also fails on concave walks: the approximation owes the shape its dents. Measured in the kit: the collider is one-sided too. A marble falls through a counter-clockwise face from above unless backface_collision is set, so a surface that shows from one side also holds from one side.
teacher.carries: Your room so far: one plane you walked, three points and one line. Commit it.
teacher.learner_room: Stand on your walk: the plane made from your own trace becomes floor; walk to its edge and look under it.

stops.title: When things go wrong: the drafter is a machine
stops.makes: You build a cube from eight corners and twelve triangles, direct a drafter under a three-line protocol, read its errors, and export your first build.
stops.image_caption: The repaired cube, from above, with the marble at rest on its top. The one-line draft looks just as whole from here; from behind it is an open room, every triangle facing inward, and the marble comes to rest inside it.

teacher.why_here: Directing generated code has no spine sequence: it is Palle's own Queer 3D practice, and every later planted bug assumes the debugger, so it closes week one. The bias hall (postfoundationscrisis, spine 25) is walked as an encounter only; it returns as a carrier at ch38. Operation added to the toolkit: build, direct, ship.
teacher.check: Axis: which draft builds the cube - my one face / the one-line draft (make a cube) / the three-line draft / the repaired draft. Predict first: From above, your one face and the three-line draft will look most alike (measured: 0.36% of the frame apart), because the draft's top is wound the wrong way and is absent. The one-line draft, wrong in every triangle, looks like a whole cube from above and like an open room from behind; a marble dropped on it comes to rest inside. Write which pair you expect, from above and from behind, before you render.
teacher.contrast: Claim: An instruction fixes what it names; naming is not checking. The draft that looks most finished from one side is the one that is wrong everywhere. Debt: Algorithmic enclosure and the default body: the assistant learned from other people's code and repeats its norms (a cube at the origin, a capsule player, OpenGL winding). Chun's 'sourcery': seeing generated source is not knowing what it does. A build is a second machine with its own errors (read-only res://, another refresh rate). Measured in the kit's first export: assert() is skipped in a release build, push_error() loses its line number there, and the exe without its .pck answers that the project data could not be loaded; what the editor told you, the build may not.
teacher.carries: SYNTHESIS I: export your room (the walked plane, three points, one line and the repaired drafted cube) and stand in it on another machine. Keep the prompt, the model's first answer and your repair in the README.
teacher.learner_room: Run your exported build on a classmate's laptop, or on the headset where one is available (the headset is an export): the first time your room exists outside your editor, and you stand in it. In the short track, the scans made on day 4 are imported by the teacher (glTF, scale fixed) and already stand in your room for this first export, so the collage reaches the headset in week one; ch18 teaches the import and makes the scan a member of your family.

stops.title: The organism: bone, tendon, muscle
stops.makes: You articulate a limb of three segments with pivots that turn by delta: the first body that moves by itself.
stops.image_caption: The limb of three bars, each joint turned, over the supplied lattice; the cube and the marble from the chapter before stand beside it. One turn of the limb carves 33 cells where the toe passes. Pass the toe position in the limb own frame by mistake and six other cells go instead.

teacher.why_here: Operation added to the toolkit: articulate.
teacher.check: Axis: where the pivot sits on each segment, same joint angles - at the end / at one third / at the centre / outside the bar. Predict first: At rest all four look the same: the pivot moves origins, not bars (measured: no pair differs on more than 0.18% of the frame). With every joint at 30 degrees, one third and the centre are the closest pair, and only the pivot at the end keeps the chain joined: the others open a gap at the knee (5 and 8 cm). Write the pair you expect, at rest and turned, before you render.
teacher.contrast: Claim: A body's motion is decided by where its joints are, not by what its parts look like. Debt: Klee maps active, medial and passive onto brain, tendon and bone, and onto male and female organs ('Male organs (anthers), active'). The scene tree encodes the same command chain: the parent moves the child, never the reverse. That hierarchy is taught here and inverted in ch21. And frames are not time: speed per frame runs 1.5 times faster at the headset's 90 Hz than at 60 Hz; delta is the repair promised in ch2. Measured in the kit: delta repairs the speed, not the sampling. At 144, 60 and 30 frames a second one turn of the limb carves the same 33 cells; at 3 frames a second it carves 26, because the foot is only asked where it is when a frame comes.
teacher.carries: Give one body in your room a jointed part that moves.
teacher.learner_room: Become it: attach the chain to your hand (headset) or the carried point and walk it through Trans_Body's lattice, carving a passage with your own movement ('chip from chip').

stops.image_caption: The process strip of the first assemblage, one still after each operation: the point, plus the walked plane, plus the cube, plus the limb, the pivots set, the same parts as a chain, and every pivot turned 30 degrees. Tiles 5 and 6 are identical to the pixel: the tree changed and the picture did not.

teacher.why_here: Operation added to the toolkit: assemble. Assemblage I.
teacher.check: Axis: how the same four parts are parented - flat: four children of the root / a chain: each part the child of the one before / a chain with offset pivots / two chains from one hip. Predict first: At rest all four look the same, and they still look the same when the root turns 30 degrees: every pair differs on 0.00% of the frame, because a root carries everything below it whatever the tree looks like. Turn every pivot 30 degrees and they part: flat and two chains stay closest (0.55% of the frame), the offset chain and two chains are farthest (4.77%), and the toe travels 0.47 m in the flat body against 2.61 m at the end of the chain. Write which pair you expect closest, and when you expect any difference at all, before you render.
teacher.contrast: Claim: The structure of an assemblage is invisible at rest and while only its root moves; it shows when a part inside moves. The tree, not the parts, says what the body does. Debt: A hierarchy is a command chain. The root moves, the leaves obey, and nothing in the picture shows who commanded whom. Klee drew it as brain, muscle, bone, active to passive; Godot draws it as a tree whose root you chose. The debt is that the choice of root is a choice of who gets to be the body's centre, and the default (the first node you made) is not a neutral one.
teacher.carries: Your room's first assemblage: at least three parts of different origin (one made in code, one drawn by hand in the editor, one carried in from a classmate's scene) under one root. Decide the root and write one line in the README saying why that part commands.
teacher.learner_room: Carry the root: pick the whole body up (XR hand or desktop carry) and the parts come with it, pivots and all. Then walk into Trans_Scale with it: the room scales by four, the body scales with the room, and the door you could not use before is usable; the body's relations survive the scale, which is what a hierarchy is for.

stops.title: The chessboard: purely repetitive and therefore structural
stops.makes: You repeat one cube into a floor by a nested loop, colour it by a rule over (x, z), and turn one cell into a ghost.
stops.image_caption: The process strip of the chessboard, one still after each operation: one cube, a row, the floor, two colours, hue by index, a ghost cell, the spacing opened. Tiles 5 and 6 are the same picture: the ghost cell looks like its neighbours, and a marble dropped on it falls through. Opening the spacing changed the picture most.

teacher.why_here: Operation added to the toolkit: repeat.
teacher.check: Axis: rhythm rule over the same 8 x 8 cubes - every cell alike / (x + z) % 2 chessboard / x % 3 stripes / hue from x + z. Predict first: Cell by cell, every cell alike and the x % 3 stripes are the closest pair: they differ in 24 of 64 cells (measured: 11.12% of the frame from the study camera). The chessboard and the stripes disagree on about half the floor (14.26%). Only when the cells are averaged away do the chessboard and the stripes come closest, and that distance was not rendered: it is arithmetic on the stills. The stripes have a direction too: swapping x and z changes 30 of their cells. Write the pair you expect before you render, and say from how far.
teacher.contrast: Claim: Structure is the repetition rule, not the cube: the same 64 bodies make four different floors. Debt: The grid is the unexamined ground of 3D (editor grids, voxels, the frame buffer as a grid, after Gaboury); it is a choice, and the standing ruling holds that the first line did not need it. HSV promises equal steps of hue, and the eye does not see them as equal: the yellow band looks brighter and wider than the blue one. Measured in the kit: the planted integer division, (x + z) / (2 * n) without float(), gives hue 0 in all 64 cells, a red floor with one warning and no error. One material made before the loops is one material on 64 cubes: change one cube and all 64 change. And the gap a body meets depends on how fast it arrives: a marble let go at 0.75 m passes when the gap equals its width, to the millimetre; dropped from 2 m it passes 2 cm earlier and, just below that, sticks between the cubes. Why it switches where it does is not explained.
teacher.carries: Lay a floor for your room with a rhythm rule of your own and two colours you chose.
teacher.learner_room: Walk the floor; turn one cell into a ghost with ch3's if and fall through it.

stops.title: Families: one body in a single class
stops.makes: You describe a body in a single class with two exported fields, so it becomes a family, and sweep one axis into a comparison sheet.
stops.image_caption: The process strip of the family: a sphere written out, the same as a class, a row of four, hung and named, the axis set by a wrong name, the right name. In tile 5 the plates read 4, 8, 16, 64 over four identical bodies; nothing in the picture says so except the bodies themselves.

teacher.why_here: return: the family is declared at the first family hall (Primitives_Ignorance), once there are many to vary (after the chessboard). Operation added to the toolkit: parameterise.
teacher.check: Axis: sphere segments (rings = half) - 4 / 8 / 16 / 64. Predict first: 16 and 64 will look most alike at 2 m (measured: they differ on 0.85% of the still from the side, 0.99% from above, and stay the closest pair lit flat, at 4.65%). Most of that likeness is smooth shading: the rim differs by a band about 3 pixels wide. From above, the outline of 16 misses the circle by 2.06% (the chord arithmetic gives 1.92%). 4 is another body, but not the octahedron: with rings at half it has two rings and 16 triangles. Write the pair you expect, and what you think the likeness is made of, before you render.
teacher.contrast: Claim: The class's integer decides which body you have, and there is no step where a sphere stops paying: against 64 the difference falls evenly, 15.27, 5.17, 0.85, 0.19% for 4, 8, 16 and 32 segments. What looks like enough is a decision about distance and light. Debt: A class's fields decide which bodies are possible (the CCSWG prompt 'describe it in a single class', turned to a body): an int cannot have 3.5 segments, and no value of rings makes a torus. Polycount against smooth deformation, the application's topology question, enters here. Measured in the kit: set() on a typed int does not refuse a text. It converts it in silence: '16' becomes 16, 'sixteen' becomes 0, '4 8 16 64' becomes 481664, and 640 passes an @export_range of 4 to 64. What set() does refuse in silence is a name the class does not have, and a number handed to a String field. So the planted fault is a wrong field name: four members come back alike under four different plates, and only the printed triangle counts say so (the Ada project's own science_screen case).
teacher.carries: Turn one of your bodies into a class with two axes; write the closest-pair prediction before rendering its sheet.
teacher.learner_room: Walk the sheet as a gallery wall; carry one member into your room.

stops.title: Collage: a found body joins the family (assemblage II)
stops.makes: You recreate Durer's truncated solid as a family member, import a scanned body beside it, and export the hybrid room.
stops.image_caption: The process strip of the collage: the cube pulled, stood on its diagonal, two corners cut, a drafted answer beside it, a found body arriving, and the found body given its unit and its origin. In tile 5 the plate marked found is empty: the body is there, 99 m high and 43 m away, and nothing says so.

teacher.why_here: return: Melencolia, the last primitives hall, closes the repeat-and-vary part as its assemblage; it needs the family and the import. Operation added to the toolkit: collage. Assemblage II.
teacher.check: Axis: how the body was made - by hand / drafted from your three lines / found (a stand-in for a scan). Predict first: By hand and drafted will look most alike, and here they are the same picture: 0.00% of the still differs from the side, from above and lit flat. The reason is not that they share primitives (one is built with SurfaceTool, the other from an indexed array); the three lines named every number the picture shows. Ask both for a value the lines did not name and they part: a cut of 0.9 is clamped by one and kept by the other, and the stills differ on 14.88%. The found body differs from the solid on about 3% and has 5,851 triangles to its 20. Whether a real scan is the outlier by count and not by silhouette is not tested here: the stand-in was made from the solid, so its outline is near by construction. Write the pair you expect, and what would make two bodies made the same way differ.
teacher.contrast: Claim: Two bodies that look the same have agreed only about what was named. How a body was made shows in what it does with a value nobody asked for, and in its triangle count. Debt: Recreation (SFPC Recreating the Past): the difference between Durer's solid and yours is where the debt is written; the Melencolia hall already says its hidden surfaces 'are decisions we have made'. The scan has millions of triangles, holes and no inside, and whose bodies scan well is not neutral (Queer 3D: stretchability, topology, bias). Measured in the kit: the import arrives 99.04 m high, its lowest point 4.3 m up and 43 m from its plate, with none of its corners in view. Godot prints no error and still reports the triangle count; the picture shows an empty plate. Scale alone does not bring it home: the file has its own origin, and that is a second fault. The drafted answer in the kit came from one question put once to an assistant of the same kind as the one that wrote the lesson, so it is not an independent witness.
teacher.carries: SYNTHESIS II and the short track's pivot: export your room as a build with your family and one found body. The mini project starts from this build.
teacher.learner_room: A hybrid room (Queer 3D's ontology layer): imported and procedural bodies share one floor. Export the build and show it.
